title.en: The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea

region.zh: 東南格陵蘭（阿馬薩利克一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (South-East Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea', eBook #28932

summary.en: A beaten, pregnant wife walks straight out into the sea and survives, building a house on the bottom; there she bears a son with jellyfish eyes, seaweed hair, and a mussel for a mouth. Grown strong from lifting stones, the boy visits the world above with his mother — who warns him to look as angry as he can — and one thrust of his monstrous head at a doorway frightens every person inside to death, a vengeance on the household where his mother once fled her husband's beatings.
summary.zh: 受虐孕婦徑直走入海中不死，於海底築屋安身；所生之子，眼為水母、髮為海藻、口如蚌殼。少年力大，能舉箱大之石。母子重返人間，母親囑其入屋時要裝出最怒的面容；他把怪頭一伸門口，屋內之人全數嚇死——那正是母親昔日逃家避打的人家。

sensitivity.note: South-East Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Domestic-violence frame presented as told in the archival source.

passages.text: It was the usual thing: the Obstinate One had taken a wife and beat her, and when he wanted to make it an extra special beating he took a box and banged her about with that. One day, nearly at her time, she ran away and walked straight out into the sea; nearly drowned, she came to herself at the bottom of the sea, and there built herself a house. While she was down there the child was born — so ugly she nearly died of fright: its eyes were jellyfish, its hair seaweed, its mouth like a mussel. And these two lived down there together.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The boy grew up able to hear the children playing on the earth above, and said he would like to go up and see. 'When you have grown stronger, then you may go,' said his mother, and he practised with stones until he could pick up stones as big as a chest and carry them into the house. One dark evening, when the children above cried out 'Iyoi-iyoi-iyoi' with all their might, she agreed to go with him — but he must not enter the houses nearest the shore, for there she had often fled in when his father would have beaten her, and there she had suffered much evil. 'When you thrust in your head, be sure to look as angry as you can.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Two houses stood on the shore, one a little way above the other. When the mother saw her son heading for the lower one — the very house where she had always run from her husband's fists — she cried out to him to go to the one above. The boy made his face fierce and thrust his head in at the doorway, and all those inside fell down dead with fright. He would have beaten his father, but his father had died long since. Then he went down again to the bottom of the sea. When day dawned, the people of the lower house came out and marvelled at footprints all full of seaweed; following them to the upper house, they found that all inside had died of fright.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'The Boy from the Bottom of the Sea'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 馬基特與獨居者的蠟燭

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Makite', eBook #28932

summary.en: A unsuccessful hunter abandons his seal-rich in-laws to live alone in the hills, sleeps in a lone-dweller's house hung with reindeer and fox skins, and learns by threat where the candle-like treasures grow — on the farther of two blue hills in the south. Surviving his host's midnight bow, he kills the pursuer with a backward-thrust harpoon, witnesses the dwarfs' wave-war with the inland-dwellers, and returns home to hang the candle-things from the high hill in his own house.
summary.zh: 獵運不濟的馬基特拋下多豹的妻族，獨自入山居住。他借宿獨居者之屋——牆掛馴鹿狐皮，屋內有如蠟燭之物——逼問得其所來：在南天兩座藍山中較遠的山頂。夜半避過主人的弓，又反手一叉殺了追兵；其後目擊矮人與內陸人鬥水成浪之戰，歸家後取回山頂蠟燭之物，懸掛屋中直至終老。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s; lone-dweller (tornit/inlander) narratives are a major cycle of Greenlandic oral literature.

passages.text: Makite took to wife the sister of many brothers, but he never managed to catch a seal in his kayak while his wife's brothers caught them in great numbers. Hearing that his wife would leave him because he never caught anything, he resolved in his grief to go up into the hills and live there all alone. When darkness fell he set off; his wife's father saw him go and cried to the house, 'Go after him' — but Makite made his steps longer and longer until the brothers gave up the pursuit. At dawn he came to a house with hangings of nothing but reindeer and foxes' skins, and went in.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The door hinge creaked and the house shook; the lone-dweller, its master, came in and offered food, but Makite would eat nothing until he learned what those candle-like things in front of the window were. 'That is no concern of one who is not himself a lone-dweller,' came the answer — until Makite threatened to kill him. Then the lone-dweller told: on the nearer of the two great blue hills away south you will find nothing, but he who climbs the farther hill and reaches the top will find such things there; but this cannot be done by one who is not a lone-dweller. During the night Makite caught the host quietly stringing his bow to kill him in his sleep, feigned waking, and at dawn slipped out; pursued, he ran three times round a big rock and thrust his harpoon out behind him without turning, striking the pursuer in the side and killing him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wandering at hazard he came to a great plain with something like a house in the middle: the house of a dwarf, crowded with folk streaming in and out, too small even to put his foot in the passage until told to heave up the passage way with his back. The old creature warned him as he went out: look towards the west, the inland-dwellers are coming. The dwarfs went out to fight, posting themselves on the plain in two silent lines; when the inlanders' dog gave a great bark, a mighty wave rolled up to the dwarfs — and shrank to nothing close by them. Then the dwarfs' dog barked, their own wave rose and washed right over the inland folk, drowning all but a few. Makite built himself a house, fetched some of the candle-like things from the high hill, hung them up in his house, and lived there until he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Makite'; not verbatim.

title.en: Asaloq: The Strength Trial and the Magic Songs
title.zh: 阿薩洛克：角力試煉與咒歌

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Asaloq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Searching for his vanished foster-brother in a three-layered umiak, Asaloq passes a black ripple of sea-lice that eats one skin layer and a ripple of sea-serpents that eats another, to land among strangers whose squint talebearer-boy betrays his presence. Summoned before their strong man, he eats until the food falls out of his stomach and pulls arms until the skin is worn from his own — leaving strongest of all — then hides on an island and sings magic songs until the pursuing umiaks give up and row home.
summary.zh: 阿薩洛克乘三層皮大舟尋找失蹤的結拜兄弟，途經海虱黑浪（蝕去一層皮）與海蛇黑浪（再蝕一層），抵達異鄉；斜眼傳話童洩其蹤。彼族力士召他比武——他大吃至腹中之物盡吐，又拉臂拉到自身皮開肉綻，終以最強者離場。北來大舟搜捕之際，他立於山頂高唱咒歌，直到追兵放棄返航。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Sea-lice and sea-serpent passages are cosmological hazards of the Greenlandic kayak world.

passages.text: Asaloq had a foster-brother who disappeared one day while he was out in his kayak. Finding him nowhere, Asaloq built a big umiak covered with three layers of skins and rowed south with his wife. A black ripple appeared on the sea ahead: the sea-lice, which ate away the outermost layer of skins before they got through. Another black ripple: the sea-serpents, which cost them a second layer. With one layer left they rowed in fear, rounded a point, and came in sight of a place with many houses, where the strangers caught hold of their boat and hauled it up for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The place had a strong man in its midst, and a squinting talebearer boy who, in spite of being set up behind the lamp, slipped out and ran to tell. Faces filled the window: 'We are sent to bid the stranger come.' In the crowded house the strong man called from the far end of the bench, 'Let us have a wrestling match'; a skin was spread on the floor and food brought in — Asaloq ate till there was no more left, and when he rose, all he had eaten fell out of his stomach. Then the pulling of arms: he pulled at the arms of all the men until the skin was worn from his own arm, the flesh almost bare. Straightening out every arm in the house, he went out strongest of all and rowed south with his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On a little island they pitched their tent on the sunny side; from the hilltop Asaloq saw many umiaks coming from the northward, which camped on the shady side, searching carefully about — 'He can hardly be on such a little island.' Asaloq sang magic songs over them from the top of the hill until he heard them say, 'We may as well go home again.' Not until they were out of sight did he row on south, and at last they reached Aluk, where their bones still rest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Asaloq'; not verbatim.

title.en: Ukaleq: Killed by the Magic Bear, Raised by His Mother
title.zh: 烏卡萊克：魔熊之殺與母親之復生

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition (West Greenland); collected by Knud Rasmussen, published 1921

source.work: Knud Rasmussen (collector), Eskimo Folk-Tales, ed. and rendered into English by W. J. Alexander Worster (Gyldendal, 1921), 'Ukaleq', eBook #28932

summary.en: Ukaleq, who never failed to kill whatever game he chased, dies at last to a Magic Bear whose teeth whisper his killing to the comrades who find him. His mother, keeping the dress he wore as a little child, hushes it in her carrying bag through five days without food or drink until it begins to crawl — and as it springs out the dead man begins to breathe and sit up, restored. At a great spirit calling, an old wifeless man's question shames the woman who owned the Magic Bear so that she dies on the spot; Ukaleq goes home and never hunts bears again.
summary.zh: 從不失手的獵手烏卡萊克終為魔熊所殺——熊齒低語向同伴揭露真相。其母藏著他幼時舊衣，將之抱於行囊中如哄嬰兒，絕食絕飲五日，直到囊中之物蠕動欲出；舊衣一躍而出，屋搖震動，死者開始呼吸、坐起，復活如初。大降靈會上，無妻老人一句質問，令養魔熊的老嫗羞死當場；烏卡萊克從此再不獵熊。

sensitivity.note: West Greenland tale recorded by Rasmussen, 1910s. Magic Bear (a tupilak-like created bear) and child's-dress resurrection beliefs documented as told in the source.

passages.text: Ukaleq was a strong man who had only to go out after whatever game was heard of, even a great bear, to kill it. One winter, hunting on the new ice, he found the bear not easily brought down; it sighted him and turned to pursue, and though he wounded it now and again as he fled, he was killed himself at last — at the same moment the bear fell dead. When his comrades came to look at it, its teeth began to whisper, and then they knew Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear. They took the dead man home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother had kept the dress he wore as a little child. She had him laid in the middle of the floor on a skin, put the dress in her carrying bag, went out to the cooking place in the passage, and said: 'For five days I will neither eat nor drink.' Then she began hushing the dress in the bag as if it were a child, hushing on and on until it began to move — and just then someone came out saying Ukaleq was beginning to quiver. She hushed still harder; the thing in the bag tried to crawl out as someone called that Ukaleq had begun to breathe and was sitting up. The bag's occupant sprang out and made the whole house shake. They made up a bed on the side bench; after five days without eating or drinking he came to himself, and commenced to go out hunting once more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next winter, when the ice had formed, the villages held their spirit callings and visited one another. Ukaleq went with his family to a big calling in a house with three windows, crowded with folk. Midway, an old woman sitting cross-legged on the bench turned and said: 'We heard last autumn that Ukaleq had been killed by a Magic Bear.' An old wifeless man turned to her at once: 'Was it by any chance your Magic Bear that killed him?' She answered, 'Mine? Now where could I have kept such a thing?' — but after saying that she did not move; she even forgot to breathe, for shame at having been discovered, and died on the spot. Ukaleq went home and never went out hunting bears again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Knud Rasmussen, Eskimo Folk-Tales (Worster 1921), 'Ukaleq'; not verbatim.
